goal.statement: Explain to a friend why light cannot escape a black hole, and roughly where the boundary sits.
goal.audience: a curious adult, no physics past school

capstone.prompt: The Sun weighs about 2e30 kg. If it collapsed, how wide would its boundary be — and why won't it?
rubric: uses light speed as the limit

kcs.label: Black holes have an event horizon that defines the boundary beyond which light cannot escape.
misconceptions: Black holes are holes in space that suck everything in.
Light can escape if it is strong enough.
The event horizon is a physical surface.

check.stem: What is true about the event horizon of a black hole?
options: It is a boundary from which light cannot escape.
It is a physical surface you can touch.
It can be crossed by strong light.
It is not a defined area.
distractorSource: The event horizon is a physical surface.
Light can escape if it is strong enough.
The event horizon is not a defined area.

kcs.label: The mass of an object influences the size of its event horizon.
misconceptions: The event horizon size is the same for all black holes.
Only very massive stars can form black holes.
A black hole's size doesn't depend on its mass.

check.stem: How does the mass of an object relate to its event horizon?
options: More mass creates a larger event horizon.
Mass has no effect on the event horizon size.
All black holes have the same event horizon size.
Only supermassive black holes have an event horizon.
distractorSource: Mass has no effect on the event horizon size.
All black holes have the same event horizon size.
Only supermassive black holes have an event horizon.

kcs.label: The Schwarzschild radius describes the size of the event horizon for non-rotating black holes.
misconceptions: The Schwarzschild radius applies to all black holes equally.
You can't calculate the event horizon for non-rotating black holes.
The formula for the Schwarzschild radius is not important.

check.stem: What is the Schwarzschild radius used for?
options: It calculates the size of the event horizon for non-rotating black holes.
It applies to rotating black holes only.
It is irrelevant to black hole physics.
It defines the event horizon for stars.
distractorSource: It applies to rotating black holes only.
It is irrelevant to black hole physics.
It defines the event horizon for stars.
